dropped.reason: Official key marks both C and D (propanal and propan-2-one) for the IR spectrum question, so the question has no single correct answer.

Underdetermined: the question gives no amounts for the gases in vessel A (the school's answer assumes amounts in the ratio 2:1:2 giving $K_{eq}=1$ and $[\text{O}_2]=1$ M, which is not stated), so the shift in equilibrium cannot be determined from the information given.

questions.question: The structure of an organic compound is shown. Which are the TWO functional groups present in this molecule?
questions.answer: The molecule is $\text{HOOC}-(\text{CH}_2)_4-\text{NH}_2$ (5-aminopentanoic acid). The $-\text{COOH}$ group is a carboxyl group and the $-\text{NH}_2$ group is a (primary) amine (C). There is no amide ($-\text{CONH}-$), ester ($-\text{COO}-$ between carbons) or $\text{C=C}$.

questions.question: Which of the following conditions would be appropriate to carry out the synthesis shown (pentan-2-ol to 2-bromopentane)?
questions.answer: Converting an alcohol to a bromoalkane is a substitution of $-\text{OH}$ by $-\text{Br}$ using a hydrogen halide, $\text{R-OH}+\text{HBr}\rightarrow\text{R-Br}+\text{H}_2\text{O}$, with heating (C). $\text{Br}_2$/UV substitutes into an alkane, $\text{Br}_2$ in water adds across a $\text{C=C}$, and $\text{HCl}/\text{ZnCl}_2$ (Lucas reagent) would be used for the chloroalkane.

questions.question: The structure of a compound is shown. What is the IUPAC name of this compound?
questions.answer: The longest chain is six carbons (hexane). Numbering from the end that gives the lowest locants to the substituents gives $\text{Cl}$ and $\text{I}$ on carbon 2 and the two methyl groups on carbons 4 and 5 ($\{2,2,4,5\}$ beats $\{2,3,5,5\}$). Substituents are listed alphabetically (chloro before iodo, methyl last), giving 2-chloro-2-iodo-4,5-dimethylhexane (A).

questions.question: The heat of combustion of butan-1-ol is $2676\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. What is the value of the heat of combustion in $\text{kJ g}^{-1}$?

Ethanoic acid ($\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$) is a weak acid with $K_a=1.74\times10^{-5}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$. $1.00$ L of a solution is prepared by dissolving $0.100$ mol of ethanoic acid in distilled water. What is the pH of the resulting solution?
questions.answer: $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$. $K_a=\dfrac{x^2}{0.100-x}\approx\dfrac{x^2}{0.100}$, so $x=[\text{H}^+]=\sqrt{1.74\times10^{-5}\times0.100}=1.32\times10^{-3}$ M and $\text{pH}=-\log(1.32\times10^{-3})=2.88$ (D).

questions.question:
The table lists some properties of the straight-chained carbon compounds W, X, Y and Z.

| Compound | Reactivity in bromine water | Solubility in water |
|---|---|---|
| W | Rapidly decolourises | Insoluble |
| X | Unreactive | Insoluble |
| Y | Unreactive | Soluble |
| Z | Unreactive | Partially soluble |

Which row best identifies the compounds W, X, Y and Z?
questions.answer: Only an alkene ($\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$) rapidly decolourises bromine water by addition, so W is $\text{C}_3\text{H}_6$ and X (unreactive, insoluble) is the alkane $\text{C}_3\text{H}_8$. Of the two alcohols, methanol (short non-polar chain, strong hydrogen bonding with water) is fully soluble (Y), while butan-1-ol, with its longer non-polar chain, is only partially soluble (Z) (A).

questions.question:
The table shows some data on four acid-base indicators.

| Indicator | pH range | Colour range |
|---|---|---|
| methyl orange | 3.1–4.4 | red–yellow |
| bromophenol red | 3.8–5.4 | yellow–blue |
| methyl red | 4.2–6.3 | red–yellow |
| phenol red | 6.8–8.4 | yellow–red |

A solution, X, is made by mixing equal volumes of $0.0002\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium hydroxide and $0.0004\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ nitric acid. Which indicator would turn pure yellow when added to a sample of X?
questions.answer: Taking 1 L of each: $n(\text{H}^+)=0.0004$ mol and $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.0002$ mol, leaving $0.0002$ mol $\text{H}^+$ in 2 L, so $[\text{H}^+]=1\times10^{-4}$ M and $\text{pH}=4.0$. Methyl orange (3.1–4.4) and bromophenol red (3.8–5.4) are inside their transition ranges at pH 4 (mixed colours), and methyl red (4.2–6.3) is below its range so is red. Phenol red (6.8–8.4) is below its range, so is pure yellow (D).

questions.question: The following organic compounds all have six carbons: A: 2,2-dimethylbutane; B: 2-methylpentane; C: 4-methylpent-2-ene. Which of the following is most likely to be correct?
questions.answer: A and B are both $\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$ alkanes with the same carbon skeleton type differing in branching, so they are chain isomers (not positional isomers). The more highly branched, more compact and symmetrical A packs better in the solid, so it has the higher melting point (B). B ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{14}$) and C ($\text{C}_6\text{H}_{12}$) have different molecular formulae, so they are not isomers at all. (Note: the school's paper says 'five carbons', but each compound has six.)
options: Compound A has a lower melting point than compound B.
Compound A has a higher melting point than compound B.
Compound B and compound C are functional group isomers.
Compound A and compound B are positional isomers.

questions.question: A $3.42$ g sample of solid $\text{Mg(OH)}_2$ is added to a $200.0$ mL solution of $0.600\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ HCl. What is the final pH of the mixture?
questions.answer: $\text{Mg(OH)}_2+2\text{HCl}\rightarrow\text{MgCl}_2+2\text{H}_2\text{O}$. $n(\text{Mg(OH)}_2)=\dfrac{3.42}{58.32}=0.05864$ mol, which can neutralise $0.1173$ mol $\text{H}^+$. $n(\text{HCl})=0.600\times0.2000=0.1200$ mol. Excess $\text{H}^+=0.1200-0.1173=0.00272$ mol in $0.2000$ L, so $[\text{H}^+]=0.0136$ M and $\text{pH}=1.87\approx1.9$ (C).

questions.question: A $50.0$ mL sample of $4.0\times10^{-3}$ M $\text{AgNO}_3$ solution is added to $50.0$ mL of $1.0\times10^{-3}$ M $\text{KIO}_3$ solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$. The $K_{sp}$ value for $\text{AgIO}_3$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $3.2\times10^{-8}$. Which row of the following table correctly predicts if $\text{AgIO}_3$ will form a precipitate and the reason for this?
questions.answer: After mixing (total volume 100.0 mL, each concentration halved): $[\text{Ag}^+]=2.0\times10^{-3}$ M and $[\text{IO}_3^-]=5.0\times10^{-4}$ M. $Q_{sp}=[\text{Ag}^+][\text{IO}_3^-]=(2.0\times10^{-3})(5.0\times10^{-4})=1.0\times10^{-6}$. Since $Q_{sp}>K_{sp}=3.2\times10^{-8}$, the solution is supersaturated and a precipitate forms (B).

questions.question: 2-methylcyclohexanol is an alcohol and undergoes a dehydration reaction with concentrated sulfuric acid as shown. What is the major organic product of this reaction?
questions.answer: Dehydration removes $-\text{OH}$ and a hydrogen from an adjacent carbon to form a $\text{C=C}$. Two alkenes are possible: the double bond can form towards carbon 2 (giving the more highly substituted alkene, 1-methylcyclohexene) or towards carbon 6 (3-methylcyclohexene). The major product is the more stable, more substituted alkene (Zaitsev), 1-methylcyclohexene, in which the methyl group is on a carbon of the double bond (A). C (an exocyclic alkene) is a less-favoured minor product and D (a ketone) would need an oxidising agent.

questions.question: Consider the following equilibrium for a weak base $\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$: $\text{N}_2\text{H}_4(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{N}_2\text{H}_5^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$. A $0.75$ mol sample of $\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$ is placed in a $1.00$ L flask. After the system comes to equilibrium, the flask contains $0.45$ mol $\text{N}_2\text{H}_5^+$. The value of $K_b$ for the weak base $\text{N}_2\text{H}_4$ is:
questions.answer: At equilibrium $[\text{N}_2\text{H}_5^+]=[\text{OH}^-]=0.45$ M and $[\text{N}_2\text{H}_4]=0.75-0.45=0.30$ M. $K_b=\dfrac{[\text{N}_2\text{H}_5^+][\text{OH}^-]}{[\text{N}_2\text{H}_4]}=\dfrac{0.45\times0.45}{0.30}=0.68$ (B).

questions.question: A food critic noticed their speciality chicken dish was extremely bland and requested that analysis be carried out to measure the sodium chloride concentration. This was achieved by dissolving the food sample in water and the chloride ion being precipitated by adding an excess of silver nitrate solution. The precipitate was washed and dried. If the mass of the food sample was $10.0$ g and the final precipitate had a mass of $0.188$ g, what is the percentage of sodium chloride in the food?
A simplified mass spectrum of butanoic acid is shown. The peak with the mass-to-charge ratio, $m/z$, of 73:
questions.answer: Butanoic acid, $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$, has $M=88$, so the molecular ion ($m/z=88$) has a greater $m/z$ than 73 even though it is not shown on this simplified spectrum (A is false). The peak at 73 is $M-15$, loss of a $\text{CH}_3$ radical, leaving the positively charged fragment $[\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}]^+$ ($3\times12+5\times1+2\times16=73$). Only positive ions are detected, so the species must carry a $+$ charge (D).

questions.question: Silver chromate ($\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4$) is a yellow solid that dissolves in water to produce a yellow saturated solution containing $2.34\times10^{-2}\ \text{g L}^{-1}$ of silver chromate. The molar mass of silver chromate is $331.8\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$. The molar concentration of chromate ions in a saturated solution of silver chromate in $0.183\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ silver nitrate is:
questions.answer: Molar solubility in water: $s=\dfrac{2.34\times10^{-2}}{331.8}=7.05\times10^{-5}$ M. $\text{Ag}_2\text{CrO}_4(s)\rightleftharpoons2\text{Ag}^+(aq)+\text{CrO}_4^{2-}(aq)$, so $K_{sp}=(2s)^2(s)=4s^3=4(7.05\times10^{-5})^3=1.40\times10^{-12}$. In $0.183$ M $\text{AgNO}_3$ the common ion gives $[\text{Ag}^+]\approx0.183$ M, so $[\text{CrO}_4^{2-}]=\dfrac{1.40\times10^{-12}}{(0.183)^2}=4.19\times10^{-11}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ (B). (Note: the school's paper gave all four options in units of $\text{g L}^{-1}$, which is inconsistent with a 'molar concentration'; the options here are given in $\text{mol L}^{-1}$, matching the values.)

questions.question: A student constructed a model to help others visualise the composition of a solution of $0.1$ M hydrofluoric acid, which has $K_a=6.7\times10^{-4}$. The student counted out 25 dark blocks (each representing a fluoride ion, $\text{F}^-$) and 25 light blocks (each representing a hydrogen ion, $\text{H}^+$). A dark block joined to a light block represents a hydrogen fluoride molecule, HF. The student used the $K_a$ value to calculate how many dark and light blocks to join so that the model has the correct percentage ionisation for the acid, then placed all single and joined blocks in a beaker. How many separate dark blocks should the student have placed in the beaker to show the correct percent ionisation?
questions.answer: $\text{HF}(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{H}^+(aq)+\text{F}^-(aq)$, $K_a=\dfrac{x^2}{0.1-x}=6.7\times10^{-4}$, so $x^2+6.7\times10^{-4}x-6.7\times10^{-5}=0$ and $x=7.9\times10^{-3}$ M. Percentage ionisation $=\dfrac{7.9\times10^{-3}}{0.1}\times100\approx8\%$. Of the 25 'HF units', $8\%$ is $0.08\times25=2$ ionised, so 2 separate dark ($\text{F}^-$) blocks (and 2 separate light blocks) are free, and the other 23 pairs are joined as HF (A).

questions.question: A student built a model of $0.1$ M hydrofluoric acid (HF, $K_a=6.7\times10^{-4}$) by placing in a beaker separate dark blocks (fluoride ions), separate light blocks (hydrogen ions) and joined dark-light blocks (hydrogen fluoride molecules). The aim was to help others visualise the composition of the solution. Four limitations of the model were suggested: I. The model should have included some differently coloured blocks to represent the proportion of hydroxide ions also present in the solution. II. The building blocks used were too big to represent actual ions and molecules. III. It did not include the most common chemical present in the $0.1$ M HF being modelled. IV. The true nature of the hydrogen ion in aqueous solution is not shown by the model. Given the aim of the exercise, which of the above statements are significant limitations of the final model?
questions.answer: The aim is to show the composition of the solution. Water is by far the most abundant species in $0.1$ M HF, yet the model leaves it out (III), and in aqueous solution the hydrogen ion exists as hydronium, $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$, not a bare $\text{H}^+$ (IV), so both are significant limitations. Hydroxide ions are present only in tiny amounts ($\approx10^{-12}$ M) so omitting them is not significant (I), and the size of the blocks is irrelevant to showing the relative proportions of species (II) (D).

questions.question: A pH probe is used to measure the pH of several buffers of known pH values to determine if the meter requires calibration. The graph shows the pH readings given by the probe for each of the known (real) pH values of each buffer. Which of the following statements is true, based on the data in the calibration graph?
questions.answer: The points lie on a line parallel to $y=x$, with the probe reading $\approx1$ pH unit higher than the real pH at every value (a constant offset). A solution with $[\text{OH}^-]=[\text{H}^+]$ has real pH 7 (at $25^\circ\text{C}$), so the probe would read about 8, not 6 (B false). The equivalence point would be read about one unit higher, not lower (C false). Because the reading is 1 higher, $[\text{H}^+]$ calculated from the reading, $10^{-(\text{pH}+1)}$, is $10$ times smaller than the true $[\text{H}^+]$ (D). A constant offset affects the accuracy (not the reliability/repeatability) of the readings, so A is not the best answer.
options: Using the probe without calibration will affect the reliability of data it gathers.
If the probe were placed in a solution with $[\text{OH}^-]=[\text{H}^+]$ it would read 6.
The equivalence point in a titration, as determined using this probe, will occur approximately one pH unit lower than the actual equivalence point.
The $[\text{H}^+]$ of a solution, as determined from its pH measured using this probe, will be 10 times lower than the actual $[\text{H}^+]$ in the same solution.

questions.question: A student performed an experiment to determine $K_{eq}$ for the following reaction: $\text{Co}^{2+}(aq)+4\text{Cl}^-(aq)\rightleftharpoons\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}(aq)$. The student adds a $0.253$ g sample of $\text{CoCl}_2$ to a solution of $6.0$ M NaCl. The value of $K_{eq}$ is $4.8\times10^{-4}$. Which of the following is the closest to the percentage of cobalt-containing species that is present as the blue $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ ion?
questions.answer: $K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Co}^{2+}][\text{Cl}^-]^4}$. The chloride is in large excess so $[\text{Cl}^-]\approx6.0$ M, giving $\dfrac{[\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}]}{[\text{Co}^{2+}]}=K_{eq}[\text{Cl}^-]^4=4.8\times10^{-4}\times6.0^4=0.622$. The fraction present as $\text{CoCl}_4^{2-}$ is $\dfrac{0.622}{1+0.622}=0.383$, i.e. $38\%$ (A). (The mass of $\text{CoCl}_2$ is not needed.)

questions.question:
Cycad fruits have been part of the staple diet of many Indigenous Australian peoples. However, these fruits contain toxins, such as cycasin and macrozamin, which are known to cause long-term neurological damage. The structures of macrozamin and cycasin are shown.

For safe consumption, the crushed powder from the cycad seeds was placed inside a woven bag. It was noted that running water was more efficient than still water in removing the toxins. With reference to structural formulae and relevant chemical principles, justify the above observation used to remove the toxins.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Macrozamin and cycasin have several polar hydroxyl ($-\text{OH}$) groups (and polar $\text{C-O}$ and $\text{N}=\text{O}$ / $\text{N-N}$ groups), so they can form hydrogen bonds with water molecules (ion–dipole/dipole–dipole forces are also possible). These strong attractions allow the toxins to dissolve in water, establishing a solubility equilibrium, e.g. $\text{cycasin}(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{cycasin}(aq)$.

In still water (a closed system) the dissolved toxin accumulates until the solution is saturated and the rates of dissolving and recrystallising are equal, so no more toxin is removed. In running water (an open system) the water containing dissolved toxin is continually carried away and replaced by fresh water, so the concentration of dissolved toxin stays low and equilibrium is never reached. By Le Chatelier's principle the equilibrium keeps shifting to the right to replace the dissolved toxin that was removed, so more and more toxin dissolves and is flushed out. Running water is therefore more efficient at removing the toxins, and crushing the seeds increases the surface area so the toxins dissolve faster.

questions.question: The graph shows the boiling points for two different homologous series of organic compounds, straight chained alkanes and straight chained alkane nitriles ($\text{R-C}\equiv\text{N}$). The two homologous series are labelled on the graph as A and B. Identify the label of A and B as either alkanes or alkane nitriles and explain the patterns of the boiling points shown in the graph.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** A (dots) shows the alkane nitriles and B (crosses) shows the alkanes.

*Trend 1: for both series the boiling point increases as the number of carbons increases.* A longer chain has more electrons and a larger electron cloud and surface area, so the dispersion forces between molecules are stronger, and more energy is needed to overcome them.

*Trend 2: at every chain length the alkane nitrile has a higher boiling point than the alkane.* Alkanes are non-polar, so only dispersion forces act between their molecules. Alkane nitriles have a polar $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ bond (nitrogen is more electronegative, so the nitrile group has a permanent dipole), so as well as dispersion forces there are dipole–dipole attractions between the $\delta^+$ carbon and $\delta^-$ nitrogen of neighbouring molecules. Dipole–dipole forces are stronger than dispersion forces of a comparable size, so more energy is needed to separate the nitrile molecules.

*Trend 3: the difference between the boiling points decreases as the chain length increases* (about $170^\circ\text{C}$ at 2 carbons, about $100^\circ\text{C}$ at 6 carbons). As the non-polar chain gets longer, dispersion forces make an increasing contribution to the total intermolecular attraction in both series, so the extra effect of the single polar $\text{C}\equiv\text{N}$ group becomes proportionally smaller.

questions.question: A $0.375$ g sample of butan-1-ol is burnt in a spirit burner to raise the temperature of $150$ g of an unknown liquid in a beaker supported on a tripod and wire gauze above the burner. The student noted that there was some soot on the base of the beaker. Outline a reason for this observation.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** The butan-1-ol underwent incomplete combustion (the flame had a limited supply of oxygen), which produces carbon (soot) and/or carbon monoxide instead of only $\text{CO}_2$, and the soot deposits on the cooler base of the beaker.

questions.question: A $0.375$ g sample of butan-1-ol is burnt to raise the temperature of $150$ g of an unknown liquid in a beaker. The temperature of the liquid rose from $25.0^\circ\text{C}$ when heating commenced to a maximum of $40.0^\circ\text{C}$ when heating was completed (see the graph). Based on prior testing, it was determined that $35.0\%$ of the heat produced by the combustion of butan-1-ol is lost to the surroundings. Using the information provided, calculate the specific heat capacity of the liquid, given that the heat of combustion of butan-1-ol is $2676\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** $M(\text{C}_4\text{H}_9\text{OH})=74.12\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so $n=\dfrac{0.375}{74.12}=5.059\times10^{-3}$ mol.

Heat released $=n\times\Delta H_c=5.059\times10^{-3}\times2676=13.54$ kJ $=13\,539$ J.

$35.0\%$ is lost, so $65.0\%$ is absorbed by the liquid: $q=0.650\times13\,539=8800$ J.

$\Delta T=40.0-25.0=15.0^\circ\text{C}$ (the maximum temperature when heating is completed is used, not the later cooling).

$q=mc\Delta T$, so $c=\dfrac{8800}{150\times15.0}=3.91\ \text{J g}^{-1}\ ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$ (i.e. $3.91\ \text{J g}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$).

questions.question: Two different compounds A and B are isomers with the molecular formula $\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$. The flowchart shows reactions involving nine different compounds (A to I). A and B each react with $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ and dilute $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ / heat; A gives only C, while B gives both C and E. C reacts with $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$ / heat to give D, and D shows no reaction with $\text{NaHCO}_3$. E reacts with $\text{H}^+/\text{KMnO}_4$ / heat to give F, and F reacts with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ to give G, H and I. Draw the structural formulae and state the IUPAC names of compounds A to I, justifying your compounds with reference to the information provided in the flowchart.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.**

| Compound | Name | Structure |
|---|---|---|
| A | but-2-ene | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}=\text{CHCH}_3$ |
| B | but-1-ene | $\text{CH}_2=\text{CHCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ |
| C | butan-2-ol | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH(OH)CH}_2\text{CH}_3$ |
| D | butan-2-one | $\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$ |
| E | butan-1-ol | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{OH}$ |
| F | butanoic acid | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}$ |
| G | sodium butanoate | $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COO}^-\text{Na}^+$ |
| H | carbon dioxide | $\text{O=C=O}$ |
| I | water | $\text{H-O-H}$ |

*Justification.* A and B are alkenes ($\text{C}_4\text{H}_8$ with one $\text{C=C}$) that undergo hydration (addition of $\text{H}_2\text{O}$ with $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$ catalyst) to form alcohols. A gives a single alcohol (C), so the double bond is symmetrical about the centre of the chain: A is but-2-ene, and the product is butan-2-ol. B gives two alcohols, so it is unsymmetrical; since one of its products is also C (butan-2-ol), B is the straight-chain isomer but-1-ene, which gives butan-2-ol (C, the major product, Markovnikov) and butan-1-ol (E).

Acidified $\text{KMnO}_4$ oxidises primary and secondary alcohols. The secondary alcohol C is oxidised to a ketone, butan-2-one (D), which does not react with $\text{NaHCO}_3$ (not an acid). The primary alcohol E is oxidised, via butanal, to the carboxylic acid butanoic acid (F). F is an acid, so it reacts with sodium hydrogencarbonate in an acid–carbonate reaction: $\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COOH}+\text{NaHCO}_3\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{COONa}+\text{CO}_2+\text{H}_2\text{O}$, giving the salt sodium butanoate (G), carbon dioxide (H) and water (I) (G, H and I in any order).

questions.question: Phenolphthalein is a common acid-base indicator with a $K_a$ of $3.0\times10^{-10}$ at $25^\circ\text{C}$. When dissolved in water, it undergoes dissociation: $\text{HIn}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{In}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)$, where HIn (phenolphthalein) is colourless and its conjugate base $\text{In}^-$ is pink. Distinct colour change for phenolphthalein occurs when half of the indicator is phenolphthalein and the other half is its conjugate base. Given that $\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log_{10}\dfrac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}$, calculate the pH at which phenolphthalein shows distinct colour change.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** $\text{p}K_a=-\log_{10}(3.0\times10^{-10})=9.52$. Half the indicator is in each form, so $\dfrac{[\text{A}^-]}{[\text{HA}]}=1$ and $\log_{10}1=0$. $\text{pH}=9.52+0=9.52$ (the pH equals the $\text{p}K_a$).

questions.question: The colour change of phenolphthalein ($K_a=3.0\times10^{-10}$, so $\text{p}K_a=9.52$) occurs over a limited range of pH and falls within $\pm1.00$ of the $\text{p}K_a$ value. In an experiment, a solution of a weak acid was titrated against a solution of strong base. It was found that the equivalence point occurred at a pH of $9.30$. Explain if phenolphthalein is a suitable indicator for this titration.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** The colour change range of phenolphthalein is $\text{p}K_a\pm1.00=9.52\pm1.00$, i.e. pH $8.52$ to $10.52$. The equivalence point pH of $9.30$ lies within this range, so the colour change (colourless to pink) will occur at the equivalence point and the endpoint will match it. Phenolphthalein is therefore a suitable indicator (as expected for a weak acid–strong base titration, where the salt formed is basic and the equivalence point is above pH 7).

questions.question: The Haber process is a method by which ammonia is produced commercially: $\text{N}_2(g)+3\text{H}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NH}_3(g)$, $\Delta H=-92\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. A vessel contains all three gases at equilibrium. The vessel is at equilibrium initially, then after 1 minute, the temperature of the vessel is increased. The system re-establishes equilibrium at the 2-minute mark. Draw a labelled diagram showing the reaction rate–time graph for the above conditions described. Explain with reference to collision theory and Le Chatelier's principle.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** See the graph: **A** (0–1 min) is equilibrium, forward rate = reverse rate (constant); **B** (at 1 min) the temperature increase makes both rates jump up at once, the reverse rate by more than the forward rate; **C** (1–2 min) the reverse rate falls and the forward rate rises until they are equal again; **D** (after 2 min) equilibrium is re-established at a higher rate than in A.

*B:* Raising the temperature increases the average kinetic energy of the particles, so more collisions per second and a greater proportion of collisions have energy $\ge$ the activation energy, so the rate of both the forward and reverse reactions increases immediately. The reverse reaction is endothermic (it has the higher activation energy), so its rate increases by a greater amount than the exothermic forward reaction. Now the reverse rate is greater than the forward rate.

*C:* By Le Chatelier's principle the system opposes the temperature increase by favouring the endothermic (reverse) reaction, which absorbs heat, so the equilibrium position shifts to the left: $\text{NH}_3$ is used up and $\text{N}_2$ and $\text{H}_2$ are formed. As $[\text{NH}_3]$ falls, the reverse rate decreases; as $[\text{N}_2]$ and $[\text{H}_2]$ increase, more collisions occur and the forward rate increases.

*D:* At 2 min the forward and reverse rates are equal again so a new equilibrium is established. It has a lower yield of $\text{NH}_3$ (and a smaller $K_{eq}$) but the rates are higher than at A because the temperature is higher.

questions.question: Hydrogen gas and iodine gas react in the reversible reaction $\text{H}_2(g)+\text{I}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HI}(g)$. Joseph adds $0.200$ mol of $\text{H}_2$ and $0.200$ mol of $\text{I}_2$ to a $1.00$ L closed container at $400^\circ\text{C}$. After 2 minutes, the system reaches equilibrium, and $0.316$ mol of HI is found in the container. At the 6-minute mark, how many moles of $\text{H}_2$ gas must be added to the container to increase the amount of HI by $0.050$ mol? The system re-establishes equilibrium after the 7-minute mark.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** *Equilibrium at 2 min:* HI formed $=0.316$ mol, so $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ each used $=0.158$ mol and $[\text{H}_2]=[\text{I}_2]=0.200-0.158=0.042$ M.

| (M) | $\text{H}_2$ | $\text{I}_2$ | HI |
|---|---|---|---|
| Initial | 0.200 | 0.200 | 0 |
| Change | $-0.158$ | $-0.158$ | $+0.316$ |
| Equilibrium | 0.042 | 0.042 | 0.316 |

$K_{eq}=\dfrac{[\text{HI}]^2}{[\text{H}_2][\text{I}_2]}=\dfrac{(0.316)^2}{(0.042)^2}=56.6\ (\approx57)$ (the temperature is constant so $K_{eq}$ is unchanged).

*At 6 min:* let $x$ mol of $\text{H}_2$ be added. HI increases by $0.050$ M, so $\text{H}_2$ and $\text{I}_2$ each decrease by $0.025$ M.

| (M) | $\text{H}_2$ | $\text{I}_2$ | HI |
|---|---|---|---|
| At 6 min (after addition) | $0.042+x$ | 0.042 | 0.316 |
| Change | $-0.025$ | $-0.025$ | $+0.050$ |
| New equilibrium | $0.017+x$ | 0.017 | 0.366 |

$K_{eq}=\dfrac{(0.366)^2}{(0.017+x)(0.017)}=56.6$, so $0.017+x=\dfrac{0.1340}{56.6\times0.017}=0.139$ and $x=0.122$ mol (using $K_{eq}=57$ gives $0.121$ mol).

About $0.12$ mol of $\text{H}_2$ must be added.

questions.question: The molar enthalpy of neutralisation of two reactions are given. Reaction 1: $\text{NaOH}(aq)+\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{NaCl}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, $\Delta H=-57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Reaction 2: $\text{KOH}(aq)+\text{HNO}_3(aq)\rightarrow\text{KNO}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$, $\Delta H=-57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Determine if the reaction between solutions of ammonia and hydrochloric acid will produce the same molar enthalpy of neutralisation value as Reactions 1 and 2. Justify your response using your knowledge of acid-base chemistry and include an appropriate chemical equation.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** No, it will not give the same value.

NaOH, KOH, HCl and $\text{HNO}_3$ are all strong electrolytes that ionise completely in water. In Reactions 1 and 2 the $\text{Na}^+$, $\text{K}^+$, $\text{Cl}^-$ and $\text{NO}_3^-$ ions are spectators, so both reactions have the same net ionic equation: $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow2\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (a Brønsted–Lowry acid donating a proton to a base). Since the same reaction occurs, they have the same enthalpy change, $-57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

Ammonia is a weak base: it only partially ionises in water, $\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$ (endothermic, a proton-transfer that requires energy), so the solution contains mostly $\text{NH}_3$ molecules and very little $\text{OH}^-$. HCl is a strong acid (it donates its proton to water, forming $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$), and the $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ reacts directly with the $\text{NH}_3$ molecules, which accept a proton: $\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$ (or $\text{NH}_3(aq)+\text{HCl}(aq)\rightarrow\text{NH}_4^+(aq)+\text{Cl}^-(aq)$). This is a different reaction from $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+ + \text{OH}^-$, and its enthalpy change also includes the energy needed for the (incomplete) ionisation of the weak base, so the molar enthalpy of neutralisation will differ from $-57.6\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$.

questions.question: A sealed vessel contains the gases $\text{SO}_2$, $\text{SO}_3$ and $\text{O}_2$ at equilibrium: $2\text{SO}_2(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{SO}_3(g)$, with equilibrium constant $K_{eq}$. Show a relationship between the reaction quotient, $Q$, and $K_{eq}$ for this system when it is at equilibrium.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** $Q=\dfrac{[\text{SO}_3]^2}{[\text{SO}_2]^2[\text{O}_2]}$ has the same form as the equilibrium expression, and when the system is at equilibrium the concentrations are the equilibrium concentrations, so $Q=K_{eq}$.

questions.question:
Consider the equilibrium system $2\text{NO}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons\text{N}_2\text{O}_4(g)$. An experiment is conducted to understand the relationship between reversibility, temperature and entropy. Data for the system:

| Temperature ($^\circ\text{C}$) | $\Delta G$ (kJ) | $K_{eq}$ |
|---|---|---|
| 100 | 8.4 | 0.067 |
| 0 | $-9.2$ | 58 |
| $-196$ | $-43.7$ | $3.8\times10^{29}$ |

It is known that when $\Delta G=0$, the reaction is at equilibrium ($K_{eq}=1$). Explain the changes that occur when the sealed tube containing the brown $\text{NO}_2$ gas is immersed in liquid nitrogen ($-196^\circ\text{C}$), in terms of reversibility, enthalpy and entropy.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** *Reversibility:* At $100^\circ\text{C}$, $K_{eq}=0.067$ is very small so the reactant ($\text{NO}_2$) is favoured. As the temperature falls, $K_{eq}$ increases (58 at $0^\circ\text{C}$ and $3.8\times10^{29}$ at $-196^\circ\text{C}$), so at $-196^\circ\text{C}$ the equilibrium lies almost completely to the right: the forward reaction is strongly favoured and almost all the brown $\text{NO}_2$ is converted to colourless $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$ (the tube loses its brown colour), and the reverse reaction is negligible.

*Enthalpy:* $K_{eq}$ increases as the temperature decreases, so the equilibrium shifts forward when heat is removed. By Le Chatelier's principle this means the forward reaction releases heat, i.e. it is exothermic ($\Delta H<0$). Cooling therefore favours the formation of $\text{N}_2\text{O}_4$.

*Entropy:* Two moles of gas become one mole of gas, so the system becomes less disordered ($\Delta S<0$). In $\Delta G=\Delta H-T\Delta S$ the term $-T\Delta S$ is positive and is large at high temperature (making $\Delta G>0$ at $100^\circ\text{C}$, non-spontaneous). At the very low temperature of liquid nitrogen $T$ is small, so the unfavourable entropy term is small and $\Delta G\approx\Delta H<0$ ($-43.7$ kJ): the forward reaction is spontaneous.

questions.question: A student prepared two solutions by mixing aqueous sodium hydroxide and ethanoic acid. Solution A was made by mixing together $25$ mL of $0.010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ aqueous sodium hydroxide with $50$ mL of $0.010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ethanoic acid. Solution B was made by mixing together $25$ mL of $0.020\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ aqueous sodium hydroxide with $50$ mL of $0.010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ ethanoic acid. ($K_a$ of ethanoic acid $=1.74\times10^{-5}$.) Compare the change in pH in Solutions A and B when a small amount of acid is added to the mixture, using equilibrium principles and the Brønsted–Lowry theory.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** The mixtures react by $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$.

*Solution A:* $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.025\times0.010=2.5\times10^{-4}$ mol; $n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})=0.050\times0.010=5.0\times10^{-4}$ mol. The base is the limiting reagent, leaving $2.5\times10^{-4}$ mol $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and forming $2.5\times10^{-4}$ mol $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ (in 75 mL, about $3.3\times10^{-3}$ M each). A weak acid and its conjugate base are present in comparable amounts, so A is a buffer: $\text{pH}=\text{p}K_a+\log\dfrac{[\text{base}]}{[\text{acid}]}=4.76+\log1=4.76$. When a small amount of acid ($\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$) is added, the Brønsted–Lowry base $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ accepts the protons: $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+(aq)\rightarrow\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$. In terms of Le Chatelier's principle, the added $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ shifts $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}+\text{H}_2\text{O}\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-+\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ to the left, removing most of it. The ratio base : acid changes only slightly, so the pH barely changes (e.g. adding $1.0\times10^{-5}$ mol $\text{H}^+$: $\text{pH}=4.76+\log\frac{2.4}{2.6}=4.73$).

*Solution B:* $n(\text{OH}^-)=0.025\times0.020=5.0\times10^{-4}$ mol $=n(\text{CH}_3\text{COOH})$, so the acid is exactly neutralised, leaving only $5.0\times10^{-4}$ mol $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ ($6.7\times10^{-3}$ M) and no ethanoic acid. This is a solution of the basic salt (not a buffer): $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-(aq)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}(aq)+\text{OH}^-(aq)$ with $K_b=5.7\times10^{-10}$, giving $[\text{OH}^-]\approx1.9\times10^{-6}$ M and $\text{pH}\approx8.3$. With no weak acid present to absorb added base and with only a small concentration of $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ formed, adding a small amount of $\text{H}_3\text{O}^+$ converts $\text{CH}_3\text{COO}^-$ to $\text{CH}_3\text{COOH}$ and the pH drops dramatically (e.g. adding $1.0\times10^{-5}$ mol $\text{H}^+$: $\text{pH}=4.76+\log\frac{4.9\times10^{-4}}{1.0\times10^{-5}}=6.45$, a fall of about 1.8 units, compared with 0.03 for A).

So the pH of buffer A changes very little, while the pH of B (not a buffer) changes greatly.

questions.question:
A manufacturer claims to have $30$–$32\%$ (v/v) ethanol in a popular brand of red wine. The claim can be verified by determining the concentration of ethanol in a sample of the red wine, using a redox back titration. The method is:

- Pipette $10.0$ mL of wine into a $250.0$ mL volumetric flask and make up to $250.0$ mL with distilled water.
- Pipette $20.0$ mL of the diluted wine into a conical flask.
- Add a $20.0$ mL aliquot of $0.040\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ potassium dichromate solution, then $10$ mL of concentrated sulfuric acid. Heat in a $45^\circ\text{C}$ water bath for 10 minutes in a loosely stoppered flask. All of the ethanol is oxidised to ethanal: $3\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}(aq)+\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}(aq)+8\text{H}^+(aq)\rightarrow3\text{CH}_3\text{CHO}(aq)+2\text{Cr}^{3+}(aq)+7\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)$.
- Add excess potassium iodide. The excess dichromate oxidises iodide ions: $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}(aq)+14\text{H}^+(aq)+6\text{I}^-(aq)\rightarrow2\text{Cr}^{3+}(aq)+7\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)+3\text{I}_2(aq)$.
- Titrate the iodine with $0.010\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$ sodium thiosulfate: $\text{I}_2(aq)+2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}(aq)\rightarrow2\text{I}^-(aq)+\text{S}_4\text{O}_6^{2-}(aq)$.

The volumes of sodium thiosulfate (mL) for samples A, B, C and D were $31.92$, $29.63$, $29.61$ and $29.62$ respectively. Given the density of ethanol is $0.789\ \text{g mL}^{-1}$, does the sample verified meet the manufacturer's claim? Support your answer with at least one relevant equation and all relevant calculations.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Sample A (31.92 mL) is not concordant with the other three, so it is discarded. Average titre $=\dfrac{29.63+29.61+29.62}{3}=29.62$ mL $=0.02962$ L.

$n(\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-})=0.010\times0.02962=2.962\times10^{-4}$ mol. From $\text{I}_2+2\text{S}_2\text{O}_3^{2-}\rightarrow\ldots$, $n(\text{I}_2)=\tfrac12\times2.962\times10^{-4}=1.481\times10^{-4}$ mol.

From $\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}+14\text{H}^++6\text{I}^-\rightarrow2\text{Cr}^{3+}+7\text{H}_2\text{O}+3\text{I}_2$: excess $n(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-})=\tfrac13\times1.481\times10^{-4}=4.94\times10^{-5}$ mol.

Initial $n(\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-})=0.040\times0.0200=8.00\times10^{-4}$ mol. Dichromate that reacted with ethanol $=8.00\times10^{-4}-4.94\times10^{-5}=7.51\times10^{-4}$ mol.

From $3\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH}+\text{Cr}_2\text{O}_7^{2-}+8\text{H}^+\rightarrow\ldots$: $n(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=3\times7.51\times10^{-4}=2.25\times10^{-3}$ mol in the $20.0$ mL aliquot.

The $10.0$ mL of wine was diluted to $250.0$ mL, so the whole flask contains $2.25\times10^{-3}\times\dfrac{250.0}{20.0}=0.0281$ mol, and this is the amount of ethanol in the $10.0$ mL of wine.

$M(\text{C}_2\text{H}_5\text{OH})=46.07\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, so $m=0.02813\times46.07=1.296$ g and $V=\dfrac{m}{\rho}=\dfrac{1.296}{0.789}=1.64$ mL of ethanol in $10.0$ mL of wine.

$\%\ \text{(v/v)}=\dfrac{1.64}{10.0}\times100=16.4\%$.

This is well below the claimed $30$–$32\%$ (v/v), so the sample does not meet (does not support) the manufacturer's claim.

questions.question:
Students repeated the ethanol analysis of the wine, using the following logbook extract.

*Procedure:* $50.00$ mL of wine extracted and diluted to $500.0$ mL; $20.00$ mL aliquot pipetted to a conical flask and titrated against $0.5022$ M $\text{KMnO}_4$ solution, which is a very powerful oxidising agent.

*Observations (chemicals):* wine diluted till clear, but $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ions are intensely purple.

*Observations (titrations):* Titration #1: on adding the first drop of titrant the contents turned pink immediately, then after a few seconds turned clear; a second drop did the same; adding titrant in a slow stream, the contents remained a very slight pink colour, and when the stream was stopped the contents turned clear immediately. Bubbles of carbon dioxide were observed on the surface of the solution. Titrant was added dropwise until the colour change was persistent for 10 seconds. Titration #2: as for #1. Titration #3: titrant added as a stream initially; the contents turned from pink immediately before turning clear. Brown solid was observed on the bottom of the flask.

Careful research into the observations led to the following findings. In the presence of a very powerful oxidising agent, ethanoic acid oxidises to carbon dioxide, thus inhibiting the reaction of $\text{KMnO}_4$ with ethanol. $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ may be present as well and it acts as a catalyst, thus can cause an incomplete reduction of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ ions, and the reduction product is $\text{MnO}_2$, a brown suspension.

Using the observations, suggest reasons as to why the data collected may or may not be accurate. In your response, include improvements to the experimental design.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** *Observation 1: bubbles of $\text{CO}_2$.* The permanganate is such a strong oxidising agent that it does not stop at ethanal/ethanoic acid but oxidises the ethanoic acid to carbon dioxide. Ethanol is therefore being oxidised to an uncertain mixture of products, so the mole ratio of $\text{MnO}_4^-$ to ethanol is not fixed or known, and extra $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is consumed by the over-oxidation. A larger titre is needed than for the ethanol alone, so the calculated ethanol content would be overestimated (inaccurate). *Improvement:* use a milder oxidising agent that converts ethanol to ethanal/ethanoic acid only, such as acidified dichromate (back titration as in part (a)).

*Observation 2: brown solid ($\text{MnO}_2$) in titration #3, and the pink colour that disappears at once.* If $\text{Mn}^{2+}$ is present it catalyses the reaction, and the $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is only partly reduced (to $\text{MnO}_2$ rather than $\text{Mn}^{2+}$). Because the reduction product is not the one assumed in the equation, the moles of electrons accepted per $\text{MnO}_4^-$ are less than expected, so more titrant is required (large titre) and the results of titration #3 are not reliable or concordant with #1 and #2. *Improvement:* ensure the solution is strongly acidic (excess $\text{H}_2\text{SO}_4$) so that $\text{MnO}_4^-$ is reduced fully to $\text{Mn}^{2+}$, or switch oxidant as above.

*Observation 3: end point.* The $0.5022$ M permanganate is very concentrated, so a single drop ($\approx0.05$ mL, $\approx2.5\times10^{-5}$ mol $\text{MnO}_4^-$) is a large amount relative to the ethanol in the aliquot, and adding it as a stream or by the whole drop easily overshoots the end point (also, the colour change is shown only after excess permanganate is added). *Improvement:* use a much more dilute titrant, a back titration, and add half-drops near the end point; repeat until concordant titres are obtained.

The data are therefore likely to be inaccurate (the titres too large), and the experimental design should be changed as above.

questions.question: An unknown compound, X, is analysed and shown to have a composition of $69.7\%$ carbon, $18.6\%$ oxygen and the remainder is hydrogen. The mass spectrum has an $M+1$ peak at $m/z=87.0$ (the molecular ion peak is at $m/z=86$) and a fragment ion peak at $m/z=28$. Calculate the molecular formula of compound X.
questions.answer: **Sample answer.** $\%\text{H}=100-69.7-18.6=11.7\%$. In 100 g: $n(\text{C})=\dfrac{69.7}{12.01}=5.80$, $n(\text{H})=\dfrac{11.7}{1.008}=11.6$, $n(\text{O})=\dfrac{18.6}{16.00}=1.16$ mol. Dividing by the smallest (1.16): $\text{C}:\text{H}:\text{O}=5:10:1$, so the empirical formula is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ (mass $86$). The $M+1$ peak at $87$ is caused by molecules containing a $^{13}\text{C}$ atom, so the molecular ion $M^+$ is at $m/z=86$. The molar mass equals the empirical formula mass, so the molecular formula is $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$.

questions.question: Compound X has molecular formula $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$. The following data were collected. Mass spectrum: molecular ion at $m/z=86$, fragment ion peak at $m/z=28$. Infrared spectrum: sharp peak at $1705\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ and no broad peak around $3200\ \text{cm}^{-1}$. Chemical tests: when Fehling's reagent (contains $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ ions) is added to a sample of X in a test tube placed in a warm water bath, no colour change is observed; when Tollens' reagent (contains $\text{Ag}^+$ ions) is added to a sample of X, no silver mirror is produced. Using the data above, identify two possible isomers for compound X. Justify your response by including an explanation proving your two possible isomers and disproving one other isomer.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** Two possible isomers are pentan-2-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_3$) and pentan-3-one ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{COCH}_2\text{CH}_3$) (3-methylbutan-2-one would also fit). One isomer that is disproved is pentanal ($\text{CH}_3\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CH}_2\text{CHO}$).

- The molecular ion at $m/z=86$ matches a molar mass of $86\ \text{g mol}^{-1}$, consistent with $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{10}\text{O}$ for all of these isomers. The fragment at $m/z=28$ can arise from the loss of a fragment such as $\text{CO}^+$ / $\text{C}_2\text{H}_4^+$ and is consistent with carbonyl-containing compounds.
- The sharp IR peak at $1705\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is a $\text{C=O}$ stretch, so the compound contains a carbonyl group (aldehyde or ketone). The absence of a broad peak around $3200\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ means there is no $\text{O-H}$ (so it is not an alcohol or carboxylic acid).
- Aldehydes are oxidised by $\text{Cu}^{2+}$ (Fehling's, giving a red precipitate) and $\text{Ag}^+$ (Tollens', giving a silver mirror), whereas ketones are not. Both tests were negative, so X is a ketone, not an aldehyde. Pentanal would give a positive result with both reagents (being oxidised to pentanoic acid), so pentanal is disproved; pentan-2-one and pentan-3-one are both ketones and are consistent with all the data.

questions.question: The flow chart summarises an industrial process for the synthesis of nitric acid. In the catalytic chamber ($700$–$800^\circ\text{C}$, Pt catalyst, high pressures): $4\text{NH}_3(g)+5\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons4\text{NO}(g)+6\text{H}_2\text{O}(g)$, $\Delta H=-950$ kJ. The mixture then passes through a heat exchanger (for cooling purposes) to an oxidation chamber ($50^\circ\text{C}$): $2\text{NO}(g)+\text{O}_2(g)\rightleftharpoons2\text{NO}_2(g)$, $\Delta H=-114\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. In the absorption chamber (water, $50^\circ\text{C}$, high pressures): $3\text{NO}_2(g)+\text{H}_2\text{O}(l)\rightleftharpoons2\text{HNO}_3(aq)+\text{NO}(g)$, $\Delta H=-117\ \text{kJ mol}^{-1}$. Unreacted NO and air are recycled back into the oxidation chamber, and the nitric acid can be further purified if higher concentrations are required. Explain THREE factors that may have been considered in the design of this industrial process. Make specific reference to the flow chart.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.**

*Use of a catalyst.* The platinum catalyst in the catalytic chamber provides an alternative pathway with a lower activation energy, so a greater proportion of collisions are successful and the reaction proceeds quickly at a practical temperature. This increases the rate of conversion of $\text{NH}_3$ and $\text{O}_2$ to NO, so the chamber can run efficiently and cost-effectively.

*Use of a heat exchanger and different temperatures.* The reaction in the catalytic chamber is very exothermic ($-950$ kJ), so the heat exchanger cools the gases (a safety measure, and the heat can be reused to save energy). The oxidation and absorption steps are also exothermic, so by Le Chatelier's principle the low temperature ($50^\circ\text{C}$) favours the forward reactions and a higher yield of $\text{NO}_2$ and $\text{HNO}_3$.

*Recycling of reactants.* Unreacted NO (and air) is recycled back to the oxidation chamber, so less raw material is wasted, which makes the process more economical and reduces pollution (NO and $\text{NO}_2$ cause acid rain and photochemical smog).

*(Other factors: high pressure favours the side with fewer moles of gas in the absorption step and increases the rate; the plant location gives access to ammonia and oxygen reactants.)*

questions.question:
A chemist discovered a bottle simply labelled '$\text{C}_5\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}$'. To confirm the molecular structure of the contents of the bottle, a sample was submitted for analysis by infrared spectroscopy and $^1$H and $^{13}$C NMR spectroscopy. The resulting spectra are shown, with the data from the $^1$H NMR spectrum in the table.

| Chemical shift (ppm) | Relative peak area | Splitting pattern |
|---|---|---|
| 5.45 | 1 | singlet (1) |
| 3.75 | 2 | triplet (3) |
| 2.50 | 2 | triplet (3) |
| 2.25 | 6 | singlet (1) |
| 1.70 | 2 | quintet (5) |

$^1$H NMR chemical shift data: $\text{R-CH}_3$ 0.7–1.3; $\text{R-CH}_2\text{-R}$ 1.2–1.5; $\text{R-CHR}_2$ 1.5–2.0; $\text{H}_3\text{C-CO-}$ (aldehydes, ketones or esters) 2.0–2.5; $\text{-CH-CO-}$ 2.1–2.6; $\text{H}_3\text{C-O-}$ (alcohols or esters) 3.2–4.0; $\text{-CH-O-}$ 3.3–5.1; $\text{R}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-}$ 3.5–5.0; $\text{R-OH}$ 1–6; $\text{R}_2\text{C=CHR}$ 4.5–7.0; $\text{R-CHO}$ 9.4–10.0; $\text{R-COOH}$ 9.0–13.0.

Draw a structural formula for the unknown compound that is consistent with all the information provided and justify your answer with reference to the information provided. (The IUPAC name is not required.)
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** The compound is $(\text{CH}_3)_2\text{N-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-OH}$ (3-(dimethylamino)propan-1-ol):

$$\underset{\text{CH}_3}{\overset{\text{CH}_3}{\text{N}}}-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{CH}_2-\text{OH}$$

*Formula:* $\text{C}_5\text{H}_{13}\text{NO}$ has no degrees of unsaturation (no rings, $\text{C=C}$ or $\text{C=O}$).

*IR:* a broad, strong absorption between about $3200$ and $3500\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is an $\text{O-H}$ stretch (alcohol); there is no strong sharp peak near $1700\ \text{cm}^{-1}$, so there is no $\text{C=O}$ (not a carboxylic acid, amide or carbonyl); absorptions just below $3000\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ are $\text{C-H}$ stretches and a strong peak near $1050\ \text{cm}^{-1}$ is consistent with a $\text{C-O}$ bond.

*$^{13}$C NMR:* there are four peaks (about $61$, $57$, $46$ and $29$ ppm) but five carbons, so two carbons are in the same environment (symmetry, the two methyl groups on nitrogen). The peaks at about $61$ ppm ($\text{C-O}$) and $57$ ppm ($\text{C-N}$) are furthest downfield as they are bonded to the electronegative O and N; $46$ ppm is the two equivalent $\text{N-CH}_3$ carbons; $29$ ppm is the central $\text{CH}_2$ bonded only to carbons.

*$^1$H NMR:* five environments, with relative areas $1:2:2:6:2=13$ H, matching the formula. $5.45$ ppm, singlet, 1H: the $\text{O-H}$ proton (no neighbours, exchanges). $3.75$ ppm, triplet, 2H: $\text{-CH}_2\text{-O-}$ next to a $\text{CH}_2$ (2 neighbours). $2.50$ ppm, triplet, 2H: $\text{N-CH}_2\text{-}$ next to a $\text{CH}_2$. $2.25$ ppm, singlet, 6H: two equivalent $\text{N-CH}_3$ groups with no neighbouring H. $1.70$ ppm, quintet, 2H: the central $\text{-CH}_2-$ with 4 neighbouring H (two adjacent $\text{CH}_2$ groups), the most shielded $\text{CH}_2$. These fragments connect as $\text{HO-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-CH}_2\text{-N(CH}_3)_2$.

questions.question: Calcium compounds such as calcium fluoride and calcium hydroxide are sparingly soluble in water. To investigate the solubility of calcium fluoride in calcium hydroxide, a student prepared a saturated solution consisting of calcium fluoride, calcium hydroxide and water. It had a pH of $12.0$. The student noted that the $K_{sp}$ of calcium fluoride at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $3.45\times10^{-11}$, and the $K_{sp}$ of calcium hydroxide at $25^\circ\text{C}$ is $5.02\times10^{-6}$. Calculate the molar solubility of calcium fluoride in the above solution at $25^\circ\text{C}$.
questions.answer:
**Sample answer.** $\text{pOH}=14.0-12.0=2.0$, so $[\text{OH}^-]=1.0\times10^{-2}$ M.

For $\text{Ca(OH)}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{OH}^-(aq)$: $K_{sp}=[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{OH}^-]^2$, so $[\text{Ca}^{2+}]=\dfrac{5.02\times10^{-6}}{(1.0\times10^{-2})^2}=0.0502$ M.

For $\text{CaF}_2(s)\rightleftharpoons\text{Ca}^{2+}(aq)+2\text{F}^-(aq)$: $K_{sp}=[\text{Ca}^{2+}][\text{F}^-]^2$, so $[\text{F}^-]=\sqrt{\dfrac{3.45\times10^{-11}}{0.0502}}=2.62\times10^{-5}$ M.

Each $\text{CaF}_2$ that dissolves gives 2 $\text{F}^-$, so molar solubility of $\text{CaF}_2=\tfrac12[\text{F}^-]=1.3\times10^{-5}\ \text{mol L}^{-1}$.
